notes:
I've written notes on all 23 verses, but some parts are missing. My searches never reached netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, the Catholic and Orthodox sites, the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org) or Pentecostal teachers in their own words (ag.org, pneumareview.com). I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings, so those are left out. Only the start of the Enduring Word page (through v. 7) loaded. For vv. 8–23 I used its summary and Guzik's devotional, so his notes are thinner there. Wesley's Notes cover every verse.

## Ephesians 1 – Research notes

**v. 1**
- **Who it was written to.** A few ancient manuscripts have a blank space where others read "in Ephesus." Some take this to mean it was a circular letter for many churches. Guzik thinks it was certainly meant for Ephesus but also meant to circulate, so readers can "put our city" in the blank. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-1/
- **Wesley:** "By the will of God" means Paul claims no merit of his own. He thought the letter was addressed to all the churches of Asia, not only Ephesus. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/
- **"Saints."** Precept Austin notes that in the Bible a saint is simply a person who has come to know Christ as Savior. Every believer is a saint by position and should become one in practice. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60094
- **"Faithful."** Wayne Barber reads it as saints who lived faithfully day to day, not just positionally. They lived saintly in this world. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60094

**v. 2**
- **Grace before peace.** Guzik says Paul knew that receiving God's grace comes before walking in peace with him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-1/
- Barber agrees: You don't have peace until you receive grace. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_11-3
- **Father and Son together.** Precept Austin notes that naming both as the source of grace and peace puts them on the same level, which it treats as a statement of Christ's deity. Eadie: Father and Son are both specified as the sources of grace and peace. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60094

**v. 3**
- **Background.** In Greek, verses 3–14 are one long sentence, which Guzik compares to an overture. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-1/
- **Spiritual, not material.** Guzik says these blessings are better than material ones and more secure. He adds that many Christians live far below them by settling for material concerns. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-1/
- Wesley sets them against the outward privileges of the Jews and the earthly blessings they expected from the Messiah. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/
- **Early church view.** Chrysostom, et al suppose that the apostle intends a special and marked contrast between the spiritual blessings of the new dispensation, and the material and temporal blessings of the old economy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_13-4
- Barber: these benefits are not something that are earthly. Believers already have them in Christ, even if they don't yet experience them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_11-3

**v. 4 – the main point where traditions differ (election)**
- **What most agree on.** Holiness is the purpose of being chosen. Guzik says any view of God's choice that weakens personal responsibility for holiness falls short. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-1/
- Ellicott: the words point to sanctification (being made holy), not justification. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/1-4.htm
- Matthew Henry: all who are chosen for happiness as the goal are chosen for holiness as the means. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/1-4.htm
- **Guzik (Calvary Chapel).** Believers are chosen before they have done anything. The reasons are "all in Him, not in us." He admits the truth "casts some shadows" when we try to fit it with human responsibility. He quotes Calvin: being chosen "in Christ" rules out all merit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-1/
- **Reformed / Calvinist.**
  - Pulpit Commentary: the verb means God "chose out" people for himself. The Father chose the heirs of salvation, selected those who were to be quickened from the dead. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/ephesians-1.html
  - Gill (Baptist): this cannot mean a national choice like Israel's, nor a choice to an office. It is an eternal choice of particular persons. https://studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/ephesians/1-4.html
  - Barnes: the word "us" points to individuals, not communities. He argues that objections to choosing individuals apply just as much to choosing nations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/1-4.htm
  - John Piper (Baptist, Desiring God) answers the view that God chose only "Christ and the church." He says the verse says God chose us. Not an undefined mass of people, but us, you and me personally. He admits verse 4 alone may not settle it. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/god-has-chosen-us-in-him-before-the-foundation-of-the-earth
  - Monergism (Schwertley) says Arminians "evade" this verse and gives Wesley's note as an example. https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/articles/onsite/schwerley_election.html
- **Wesleyan / Methodist / Arminian.**
  - Wesley: "us" means Both Jews and gentiles, whom he foreknew as believing in Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-1.html
  - Seedbed: in the Wesleyan view grace can be resisted, and God corporately predestines all those who respond in faith to salvation, and by foreknowledge he knows who will respond. https://seedbed.com/predestination-and-gods-sovereignty/
  - Arminius: because we are chosen "in Christ," and God sees no one in Christ unless joined to him by faith, election is peculiar to believers. https://wesley.nnu.edu/arminianism/the-works-of-james-arminius/volume-3/examination-of-a-treatise-on-predestination/
  - H. Orton Wiley (Nazarene): the proof that someone is chosen is not in the secret counsels of God, but in the visible fruits of holiness. https://wesley.nnu.edu/other-theologians/henry-orton-wiley/h-orton-wiley-christian-theology-chapter-26/
- **Ellicott (Anglican commentary series), in between.** The verse refers to all church members without distinction. He notes that when Jesus "chose" the Twelve, he added "one of you is a devil," showing that choice was not final. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/1-4.htm
- **Word order.** Ellicott thinks "in love" goes best with verse 5 ("in love he predestined us"). Guzik and Clarke keep it with verse 4, stressing that holiness means nothing without love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/1-4.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-1/

**v. 5**
- **Adoption.** Guzik quotes Barclay on Roman adoption: the adopted son got full rights in the new family and lost all ties to the old, even his debts. Stott suggests this gives believers a dignity even higher than creation gave. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-1/
- **Wesley.** God decided in advance that all who later believed would be sons. "Good pleasure" means his fixed purpose to bless all who believe, "and those only." https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/
- **Spurgeon (Baptist).** On "the good pleasure of his will": "According to the good pleasure of his will." He does as he pleases. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60109/

**v. 6**
- **"Accepted in the Beloved."** Guzik says the Greek word means "highly favored," the same word used of Mary in Luke 1:28. He quotes Chrysostom: it is like changing a leper into a lovely youth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-1/
- Precept Austin: the phrase speaks of our justification, of Christ's righteousness imputed to our account by grace through faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60109/
- **A repeated refrain.** "To the praise of his glory" comes after the Father's work, the Son's (v. 12) and the Spirit's (v. 14). https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60109/

**v. 7**
- **Redemption.** Guzik: redemption always means a price is paid, and here the price is Christ's death in our place, not his moral example. He warns against a superstitious view of "the blood." What saves is Christ's full payment, not the physical substance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-1/
- **Guzik on Luther.** In a Reformation Day piece he says Luther pointed the church back to this verse against the sale of indulgences. https://enduringword.com/martin-luther-and-the-forgiveness-of-sins/
- **Wesley.** We have redemption from the moment we believe, from both the guilt and the power of sin. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/

**v. 8**
- Guzik: some think it unwise of God to pour out forgiveness on guilty sinners, but he did it in all wisdom and prudence. https://enduringword.com/martin-luther-and-the-forgiveness-of-sins/
- Wesley: the wisdom is God's, shown in his plan of salvation. The understanding is something God works in us, so we can know and do his will. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/

**v. 9**
- Guzik: the "mystery" is God's plan, once hidden and now revealed in Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-1/
- Wesley: it is the plan of salvation by faith, only dimly shown under the Law and still hidden from unbelievers. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/

**v. 10**
- Guzik: the word for "bring together" was used for adding up a column of figures. God will make everything "add up" in Christ, either through Jesus as a Savior or Jesus as a Judge. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-1/
- Wesley: the sense is to sum up, reunite and put back in order under Christ, here meaning angels and believers, living or dead. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/

**v. 11**
- **Wesley.** "We" means Jews. God's will is the unchangeable decree "He that believeth shall be delivered." It is not an arbitrary will, but flowing from the rectitude of his nature. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ephesians-1.html
- **Spurgeon.** He argues that God, who orders providence, must also order grace: Shall the shell be ordained by wisdom and the kernel be left to blind chance? https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60096/

**v. 12**
- **"The first to hope."** Wesley takes this as Jewish believers who believed before the Gentiles. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/
- Wiley agrees: it means believing Israel, and the "you also" of v. 13 extends those privileges to Gentiles. https://wesley.nnu.edu/other-theologians/henry-orton-wiley/h-orton-wiley-christian-theology-chapter-26/
- **Wesley on predestination.** He calls this "true gospel predestination": a believer is chosen for salvation (if he endures to the end,) and appointed to walk in holiness. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/

**v. 13 – the second main debate (the "seal" of the Spirit)**
- **Sealed at the moment of faith (most evangelicals).**
  - Guzik: God's choice does not exclude human response, since the chosen also heard and believed. Sealing comes after believing, not before. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-1/
  - Precept Austin says the KJV "after that ye believed" is misleading because the Greek has no word for "after." It quotes Gaebelein: sealing is not an emotional feeling or some mysterious inward experience. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_113-14
  - Bible Hub's study page: The aorist tense for sealing places it simultaneously with faith, not as a later "second blessing." https://biblehub.com/q/What_is_being_sealed_by_the_Spirit.htm
  - Ligonier (Reformed) says Pentecost and later outpourings in Acts do not teach a "second blessing." There is no such thing as a new covenant believer who lacks the Holy Spirit. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/holy-spirit-baptism
  - GotQuestions: Rather than a mere mark, Christians are sealed with a Person. https://www.gotquestions.org/sealed-with-the-Holy-Spirit-of-promise.html
- **A later or distinct experience (older commentators).**
  - Wesley: sealed "probably some time after their first believing." The seal means a full stamp of God's image and full assurance of his promises. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/
  - Gill (Baptist): sealing is what follows believing, so true faith can exist before it. He calls it the Spirit's assurance, not baptism or the Lord's Supper. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/1-13.htm
  - Barnes links it to Acts 19, where believers received the Spirit and spoke in tongues. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/1-13.htm
  - Ellicott compares the order with Pentecost (Acts 2:38): first faith, then a special gift of the Holy Spirit. https://biblehub.com/ephesians/1-13.htm
- **Baptism and confirmation.**
  - The Cambridge Bible notes that the early Church Fathers often used "seal" to mean baptism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/1-13.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary allows the seal may be given with baptism but says it is not the same thing as baptism. https://biblehub.com/ephesians/1-13.htm
  - Meyer's commentary says the full gift of the Spirit came after baptism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/1-13.htm
  - Ligonier: baptism reflects the sealing, but only those with faith are truly sealed. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/holy-spirit-baptism
  - A Gospel Coalition writer notes that Others identify the seal with confirmation. He argues that water baptism fits as the visible sign. https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/detrinitate/what-is-the-seal-of-the-holy-spirit/
  - GotQuestions says the "true meaning of confirmation" is the Spirit's inner witness. https://www.gotquestions.org/confirmation.html

**v. 14**
- **The "pledge."** Wesley calls the Spirit both a pledge and a foretaste. The "redemption" is the church's final rescue from all sin and sorrow. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/
- Precept Austin: the Spirit is a "first installment" to assure us that our full inheritance as children of God will be delivered. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_113-14
- **Eternal security.** Some writers quoted there conclude the Spirit could never leave a heart he has sealed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_113-14
- Wesley, by contrast, adds the condition of enduring to the end (v. 12). https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/

**vv. 15–16**
- Wesley: what Paul heard was that their faith and love were lasting and growing. He prayed this way for all the churches. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/
- Lehman Strauss: Paul's prayers are included by the Holy Spirit as a corporate part of the epistle. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_115-17

**v. 17**
- **What Paul asks for.** Guzik: not special gifts or prophetic powers, but that they would know God better. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-1/
- Wesley: this wisdom and revelation is "common to all real Christians." https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/
- **"Father of glory."** Adam Clarke takes it as the giver of the glory believers expect. He allows it may simply mean "glorious Father." https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60100/

**v. 18**
- Wesley: the eyes of the heart are opened and then enlightened by the Spirit, so believers know by experience what God has called them to hope for. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/
- Barber treats this verse as the theme of the whole chapter. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_11-3

**vv. 19–20**
- Guzik: if the cross is the greatest display of God's love, the resurrection is the greatest display of his power. That power is towards those who simply believe, for now and not only after death. https://enduringword.com/when-he-raised-him-from-the-dead/
- Wesley: the same power that raised Christ gives life to dead souls and keeps them alive, "for no less would suffice." https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/

**v. 21**
- Wesley: Christ has authority over all demons, angels and earthly rulers. We know the king is above all even if we cannot name every officer of his court. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/

**v. 22**
- Wesley: Christ is head of the church both in guiding and governing it and in giving it life. Its members receive strength from him as a body does from its head. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/

**v. 23**
- **Who is "the fullness"?** Wesley finds it hard to see how the church could be the "fullness." He refers the phrase to Christ, who is the fullness of the Father. This differs from the usual reading, which takes the church as the fullness. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-ephesians/
